title: As Michigan gets an ugly win to celebrate, does Oklahoma have the bigger QB question?
content:
ANN ARBOR, Mich. — Maybe the wrong quarterback was under the microscope this week.

Michigan’s Bryce Underwood took plenty of heat for his performance in Week 1, but it was Oklahoma’s John Mateer who made the crucial mistake in Saturday’s showdown between the Wolverines and No. 11 Sooners.

Mateer’s fourth-quarter interception, thrown directly into the arms of Michigan cornerback Jyaire Hill, broke a deadlock between two offenses that struggled to score and helped the Wolverines secure a 17-10 victory in front of a large contingent of Sooner fans at Michigan Stadium.

The controversy surrounding Michigan’s win against Western Michigan, decided on a Hail Mary after officials put one second back on the clock, threatened to overshadow this Big Ten-SEC showcase. The Wolverines bounced back with a gritty, defensive-minded performance that was right in line with coach Kyle Whittingham’s style.

Here are our instant takeaways.

Underwood’s job security was a major storyline after Whittingham said his quarterback needed to “turn a corner.” Did Underwood turn that corner Saturday? Not entirely, but at least he turned the wheel in the right direction.

Underwood, the No. 1 recruit in the Class of 2025, looked much more comfortable operating Michigan’s offense than he did a week ago against Western Michigan. Offensive coordinator Jason Beck gave Underwood more opportunities to use his legs by rolling him out of the pocket and calling more designed runs. Underwood’s 38-yard touchdown run in the first quarter showed why the Wolverines want to feature him as a runner after his usage was often limited last year (especially in a loss to the Sooners). He was the Wolverines’ leading rusher Saturday with 87 yards on 18 carries and completed 9 of 17 passes for 111 yards with no interceptions.

Those numbers aren’t spectacular (he completed just 2 of 4 passes for 15 yards in the second half) but they represent a step forward from last week. At no point did Michigan seem tempted to give backup Tommy Carr a series to jumpstart the offense. The Wolverines still have issues, and Underwood’s limitations as a passer put a ceiling on the offense. This blueprint — safe passes and a heavy dose of quarterback runs — will be good enough to beat a few teams in the Big Ten. — Austin Meek

Mateer will receive (and deserve) criticism for his overall performance. His third-and-9 interception in the fourth quarter was disastrous and set up Michigan’s go-ahead touchdown, and he missed an open Rocky Beers on a crucial fourth down just past midfield late. His final numbers — 17-of-33 passing for 189 yards, 13 rushes for 45 yards — were unimpressive. He looked more like a quarterback who struggled during the back half of last season after a hand injury than the one who arrived in Norman from Washington State with a lot of hype and was a September Heisman Trophy candidate this time last year.

But Oklahoma’s offense has other issues, too. The Sooners committed three holding penalties in the fourth quarter alone because they couldn’t block Michigan’s defensive front. OU rushed for only 100 yards and 3.4 yards per carry. Those problems were the continuation of a trend from last season when the Sooners were No. 118 nationally in yards per rush (3.54). In their past five games against Power 4 opponents, the Sooners’ average yards per carry: 2.6 vs. Alabama, 3.2 vs. Missouri, 2.7 vs. LSU, 1.7 vs. Alabama (in the Playoff) and 3.4 Saturday.

Explosive receiver Isaiah Sategna III was a non-factor (five offensive touches, 20 yards). Oklahoma advanced past the Michigan 45 only three times in 11 series. Even though Brent Venables’ defense looks strong, Oklahoma is not going to be a factor in the SEC with an offense that looks this shaky. — Matt Baker

There was nothing pretty about Michigan’s performance. The Wolverines committed way too many penalties (11 for 90 yards) and gained only 75 yards in the second half. The outcome might say more about the Sooners’ flaws than it says about Michigan’s strengths. Still, Oklahoma beat Michigan soundly en route to the College Football Playoff last season and returned quite a few key pieces, including Mateer. Every single Michigan fan would have signed up for an ugly win against the Sooners when they looked at this year’s schedule.

It would have been easy for Michigan’s season to spiral after the Wolverines came within a second of losing to Western Michigan. This win should drown out much of the negativity that surrounded the Wolverines this week and give them room to make something out of Whittingham’s first season. That won’t be easy with a daunting schedule ahead, including games against Iowa, Penn State, Indiana, Oregon and Ohio State. The Wolverines can’t count on many easy wins, but they can celebrate an ugly one. — Meek

The Sooners entered with a 36 percent chance to make the College Football Playoff for a second consecutive season, according to The Athletic’s projections. It’s too early to say OU is doomed, but the road ahead looks daunting, if not impossible to traverse.

Oklahoma still has five games against currently ranked teams, starting in two weeks against Georgia. Texas, Ole Miss, Texas A&M and Missouri remain after that, plus a trip to Florida in November. Unless extreme chaos reigns this season — always possible — the Sooners can afford, at most, two losses in those games. Unless Saturday was an ugly fluke, Oklahoma does not look like a team capable of navigating that stretch with only a pair of defeats.

If that unlikely scenario happens, we’ll hear SEC-centric pundits talking up this Michigan game as a quality loss. But remember, too, that the Wolverines’ Week 1 triumph over Western Michigan should continue to be litigated (metaphorically, not literally, we presume) in future CFP discourse.

The Sooners earned their Playoff spot last year with a win at Alabama, but they never looked like a threat to make a deep run. After Saturday’s performance, it appears as if we can cross Oklahoma off this year’s list of serious contenders. The Sooners might end up being a pretty good team, but they’re nowhere near a great one. — Baker

The Wolverines close nonconference play at 3:30 p.m. ET next Saturday against UTEP, whom Oklahoma beat 51-0 in Week 1. Iowa visits the Big House on Sept. 26.

The Sooners host a Saturday night game against New Mexico before a pair of top-five SEC foes in Georgia on Sept. 26 and Texas on Oct. 10.

This story will be updated.
